examples.question_text: A male weighing $84\text{ kg}$ consumes $5$ standard drinks over $2.5\text{ hours}$. Use $\text{BAC}_{\text{male}}=\dfrac{10N-7.5H}{6.8M}$ to calculate his estimated BAC, correct to 3 decimal places.

A female weighing $66\text{ kg}$ consumes $4$ standard drinks over $2.5\text{ hours}$. Use $\text{BAC}_{\text{female}}=\dfrac{10N-7.5H}{5.5M}$ to calculate her estimated BAC, correct to 3 decimal places.

A male weighing $88\text{ kg}$ consumes $N$ standard drinks over $4\text{ hours}$. Using $\text{BAC}_{\text{male}}=\dfrac{10N-7.5H}{6.8M}$, find $N$ when his estimated BAC is exactly $0.05$. Round to 2 decimal places.
examples.solution_text:
$\begin{aligned}\text{BAC}_{\text{male}}&=\frac{10N-7.5H}{6.8M}\\0.05&=\frac{10N-7.5(4)}{6.8(88)}\\29.92&=10N-30\\59.92&=10N\\N&=5.992\\N&\approx5.99\end{aligned}$

The model gives approximately $5.99$ standard drinks.

examples.question_text: A female weighing $70\text{ kg}$ consumes standard drinks over $4\text{ hours}$. Using $\text{BAC}_{\text{female}}=\dfrac{10N-7.5H}{5.5M}$, find the maximum whole number of standard drinks for which her estimated BAC is strictly below $0.05$.
examples.solution_text:
First find the boundary where the estimated BAC equals $0.05$.

$\begin{aligned}0.05&=\frac{10N-7.5(4)}{5.5(70)}\\19.25&=10N-30\\49.25&=10N\\N&=4.925\end{aligned}$

For fixed mass and drinking time, estimated BAC increases as $N$ increases. Therefore $N<4.925$, so the maximum whole number is $4$ standard drinks.

examples.derivation: 6.8(88) = 598.4. Multiplying the substituted equation by 598.4 gives 29.92 = 10N − 30, hence 10N = 59.92 and N = 5.992 ≈ 5.99 to 2 decimal places.

5.5(70) = 385. At the boundary, 0.05(385) = 10N − 30, giving N = 4.925. The positive denominator makes BAC increase with N, so the strict condition requires N < 4.925. The greatest permitted whole number is 4.
